Miscarriage of Justice: Birth of Death

By: Diana Lucas | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
One woman's fight for the right of mothers to bury their chill whatever their age

Summary:
“The birth of death”
Sonja Smith, a Funeral Director from Centurion, is the driving force behind a forthcoming court application to challenge the law (Births and Deaths Registration Act, Act 51 of 1992) regarding miscarried babies born asleep under the age of 26 weeks of gestation who may not have a funeral and is regarded as medical waste in terms of the Waste Act.
Sonja is also the founder of a non-profit company called Voice of the Unborn Baby. It has a Facebook page and has already collected 2,000 signatures in support of the proposed court case.
Thursday 15 October 2015 is, internationally, Pregnancy and Infant Loss Remembrance Day, and this proposal relates to an insert that would ideally air on Sunday 11 October in order to coincide with this day.


Further information:
Thursday 15 October 2015 is, internationally, Pregnancy and Infant Loss Remembrance Day, and this proposal relates to an insert that would ideally air on Sunday 11 October in order to coincide with this day.
THE LEGAL CHALLENGE
Advocate Donrich Jordaan, an expert in biolaw and human rights who recently succeeded in challenging the SA Surrogacy laws and also acted for Adv. Robin Stransham-Ford in the Pretoria High Court case relating to his assisted suicide, will be representing the applicant/s in a legal challenge to the following legislation:
➢➢Births and Death Registration Act2 ➢➢Waste Act3 ➢➢Choice on Termination of Pregnancy Act4 ➢➢National Health Act5
HOW IT STARTED
A hospital threw away, in the red anatomical medical waste bin, triplets born at twenty weeks of gestation in circumstances where the parents were told that the babies would have a funeral. The babies had to be retrieved from the medical waste incineration plant by the Unit Manager of the Private Hospital6.
Sonja’s daughter also miscarried a baby.
In France, for example, miscarried and stillborn babies are given: (i) a name, (ii) and identity number, (iii) an entry in the Population Register, and (iv) permitted to have a funeral – irrespective of the gestation period.
MISCARRIAGE OR STILLBIRTH
The following paragraph sets out the position in the United States:
Both stillbirth and miscarriage are types of pregnancy loss, but they differ by when the loss occurs. A miscarriage (sometimes called a spontaneous abortion) is when a baby dies before the 20th week of pregnancy. Stillbirth is the death of a baby after the 20th week of pregnancy but before delivery.
According to South African law it is, in both instances, the twenty-sixth week.
Miscarriage has been described as “the most unrecognized loss”. Regard needs to be had to the bonding process that a mother goes through: 
THREE CASE STUDIES
1. Case Study #1 Felicia van Niekerk:
A passionate mother who will be an excellent visual case! She lost one ‘baby’ at 25 weeks and another one at 23 weeks of gestation.
Both she and her husband were fighting with everything in them to get the bodies of the ‘babies' released from the hospital for burial.
She managed to obtain Death Certificates for both ‘babies'. Her Gynaecologist was Dr Ceris, near Eugene Marais Hospital in Pretoria and he was very sympathetic towards her & her circumstances.
Her first baby was born in the ‘Moedersbond’ and the 2nd one at Life Eugene Marais Hospital.
She now has 2 boys, aged 6 and 2 yrs old and has been wanting to do something about the current legislation for the past 5 years!
Sy has a lot of ‘visuals’ at home - photo’s, sonar photo’s, memory box, etc.


2. Case Study #2 Christopher Fitchet
This is the case of 2 gay men who elected to make use of the services of a surrogate mother.
They were expecting twins, of which the one was born at 23 weeks and the other one at 25+ weeks.
The one (Lutz) was treated as medical waste and the other one (Anja) had a dignified funeral, even though they were conceived together.
They have now adopted 2 sons and were very emotional to talk about this again..

4. Case Study #4 Nicolene Eager
Nicolene resides in Pretoria East. She lost her little boy, Ryno at 22/23 weeks. Her Gynae agreed to sign the paperwork.
She keeps Ryno’s ashes on her dressing table.
She has a young daughter and has since given birth to another little boy

Press Release:


Miscarriage of Justice
Babies miscarried under the age of 26 weeks are deemed medical waste and may not be released for burial according to South African law. For many mothers, the shock discovery that they cannot plan a funeral compounds the devastating feeling of loss, and deprives them of a critical step in the healing process. But these unborn babies may soon have a voice. Carte Blanche meets Sonja Smith, the driving force behind a forthcoming court application to challenge this law.
NOTE: ALL CASE STUDIES CAME VIA SONJA SMITH - NO CONTACT NOS. FOR THEM.


Script:


STRUCTURE:

V/O 9 sec

When Nicolene Eager found out the gender of her second child, she and her husband, Schalk were thrilled, they decided to name him Ryno.

Nicolene: We found out 12 weeks it was a boy, so Dad was super happy

LINK
At 20 weeks Nicolene’s doctor told her there were problems with the pregnancy, five weeks later on 26th July 2012 Nicolene lost her baby.

Nicolene: The worst thing imaginable is to hold a lifeless bay in your arms, the hospital were so accommodating, they cared for him as if he was alive I got to keep him with me for a full 24 hours
Devi: What were those 24 hours like for you?
Nicolene: I remember telling my husband that there was no time for tears because this is the only time I have with him so there cant be tears. It was extremely sad to have to give my baby away and to know that is it. I won’t see him again…

LINK
Lying in hospital spending those last few precious moments with her baby Nicolene had no idea what was going on behind the scenes, her gynecologist signed the notification of death putting, herself at great risk.

V/O 13 sec
By signing this notification of death, the gynecologist put herself at professional risk because Ryno, born at 25 weeks, was, legally speaking, not entitled to a funeral.

Link
Current legislation states that if a baby is born under 26 weeks without taking a single breath than the body has to be disposed of as medical waste.

V/O
Hospitals for the most part, try and lessen the suffering.

Link
The parents are given the option of spending time with their baby, but the stark reality is once that time is over the baby is wrapped in a red plastic bags and placed in one of these buckets depending on weight.

Nicolene : We had no idea that there was a law how can you ever grieve and get peace in you life knowing your baby was thrown in a dustbin or bag… at least we know he was cremated in a blanket with a teddy bear
Sonja: Babies born at 25 weeks and 6 days end up as medical waste and are being incinerated with amputated limbs and other organs I cannot understand how this is defined.

LINK
For Sonja Smith a funeral Director from Pretoria it all started 10 years ago when she received a call from a hospital asking her to pick up triplets which were miscarried at 20 weeks

Sonja : When I got to the hospital, they were missing and I said you just called me to come and collect them and the answer was that the medical waste truck had already collected them for incineration.

V/O
This haunted Sonja for years and in 2005 decided to fight for new legislation.

Devi: What are you fighting for what would you like to see happen?
Sonja: I have a problem with parents not being given the choice I want to bury my baby miscarried at 20 weeks Why Not what harm does it do anyone.

V/O
A surrogate mother conceived for Christopher Fitchet and his partner.

Christopher: I received the message you have good news and bad news were pregnant and bad news twins double trouble

V/O
But the one twin, Lutz, did not survive and arrived at 23 weeks.

Christopher: I arrived at hospital lying in kidney bowl no dignity no respect. … we were told we were not able to take Lutz remains, the hospital would get rid of him as medical waste.

V/O 6 and ahalf
And all their focus was on, Anja, who was born at 25 weeks and 6 days.

Christopher: They rushed her to neonatal ICU ward… she was 23 cm quiet big for a premature baby and she was fine they put her on oxygen. She used to get excited when I walked in to the ward and she used to grab my finger and already there was this bond there was this instantaneous bond I never thought possible to immediately love a child but you do

V/O
But Anja only lived for 7 days.

Devi Now you have lost both babies
Christopher: Now we have lost both babies.

V/O
Whilst Anja was eventually able to get a death certificate and so be afforded a funeral, Lutz was termed a miscarriage.

Christopher: Anya received a death certificate and for Lutz absolutely nothing he never existed..
Devi How do you feel about the fact that this is the law?
Christopher: It angers me, the day after Lutz passed away when Anya passed away I put his pebbles in the casket with her so for us they are both there so we buried both our children.

V/O
Since the death of their twins Christopher and his partner have expanded their family they have two sons Jordan and Lentz.

Sonja: If you look at the youngest surviving premature baby that was born in the Cape was Allegra Lategan born in the Cape at 22 weeks gestation she lives, if she died she would have been medical waste.

V/O
In her quest to change this legislation, Sonja went to parliament in 2012, she has formed a non profit company called ‘Voice of the Unborn Baby’, support for her cause has magnified through it’s facebook page.

Attorney Renaldi Ingram has taken on this case pro bono. For Renaldi the fact that abortion after 20 weeks is not legal, because of the viability of the foetus, is totally contradictory to the legislation regarding the burial of babies.

Renaldi: In terms of the termination act they see viability as 20 weeks so you can decide to have an abortion and to terminate your pregnancy up to 20 weeks after 20 weeks you are not allowed to do that so there is a huge gap between the termination act and other legislation saying under 26 weeks you may not bury or cremate your baby.

Link
When Felicia’s son Deon was born at 25 weeks it was touch and go, five traumatic days later he took his last breath.

Felicia: I sat with him for a couple of minutes and then I just went outside and phoned my Dad and said its over.

V/O
Felicia was also told her baby could not have a funeral but would be disposed of as medical waste

I told them how can he be medical waste, Don’t I get a funeral. So they told me no he’s not human he is not seen as an individual

V/O
But legally if one breath is taken it’s a baby and so Deon was eventually given a funeral.

Devi: Tell me about the funeral?
It was beautiful, we had doves, It gave me comfort you need to do that to get some closure to say this is my baby I’m giving you away.

V/O
Six years down the line, Felicia now happily married to Francois, was pregnant again. But at 23 weeks she found herself, once more in a life threatening situation, her son Adrian was born dead.

Felicia: I asked them to please give him immediately to my husband.
Francois: I could hold my boy he was literally a foot long, a foot and a half

V/O 6sec
Francois on speaking to the medical staff was told their son would be disposed of but there was no way Francois was going to let that happen.

Francois: I said NO we buried her first child we would like to bury this child as well, they said they couldn’t do it because they were not allowed. I said call your security see if you will stop me and the next minute the Dr walks in, he said give me the book took it and wrote out a death certificate there done.

Sonja: In a way you are at the mercy of the hospital staff and the Dr they make these choices for you.

V/O
There is a way around the law for bereaved parents they can sign an affidavit saying that for cultural or religious reasons they are removing the placenta or human tissue from the hospital.

Devi Can you get away with it if you sign the affidavit?
Sonja: Yes
Devi: So people watching this programme will say what’s the big deal?
Sonja: Where’s the dignity.

V/O
The legal team are in the process of engaging with the Ministers involved, if necessary, Sonja is prepared to go to the constitutional court, all at her cost.

Devi : Do you understand how expensive this is going to get?
Sonja: I do am willing to go to highest courts to get this through this is my legacy that I will leave behind.

V/O
Francois and Felicia together with their sons 6 year old Francois and now 2 year old Adrian regularly visit the graves and by doing that find closure as a family

Francois: I had a conversation with a lady also at 24 weeks she lost the baby she chose that she didn’t want to see the baby they must take it away that’s her way of coping with it every person has there own way of coping with it we wanted to bury our child and that should be our choice

Promo 10

Is it fair to refuse parents the right to bury their baby, if born asleep under 26 weeks, this is the law in South Africa today.

Promo 15 sec

V/O 11 sec
Babies born dead under the age of 26 weeks are treated as medical waste Meet a woman determined to give parents the right to bury their children whatever their age.

Up Sound Sonja“ a miscarriage is the most unrecognized loss in our society.”

Promo 3 15 sec
Nicolene: How can you ever grieve knowing you baby was thrown in a bag.

V/O 7 sec
Bereaved parents speak out about the law that prevents them from burying their babies if born under 26 weeks.

V/O Felicia was also told her baby could not have a funeral but would be disposed of as medical waste I told them how can he be medical waste, Don’t I get a funeral. So they told me no he’s not human he is not seen as an individual V/O But legally if one breath is taken it’s a baby and so Deon was eventually given a funeral. Devi: Tell me about the funeral? It was beautiful, we had doves, It gave me comfort you need to do that to get some closure to say this is my baby I’m giving you away. V/O Six years down the line, Felicia now happily married to Francois, was pregnant again. But at 23 weeks she found herself, once more in a life threatening situation, her son Adrian was born dead. Felicia: I asked them to please give him immediately to my husband. Francois: I could hold my boy he was literally a foot long, a foot and a half V/O 6sec Francois on speaking to the medical staff was told their son would be disposed of but there was no way Francois was going to let that happen. Francois: I said NO we buried her first child we would like to bury this child as well, they said they couldn’t do it because they were not allowed. I said call your security see if you will stop me and the next minute the Dr walks in, he said give me the book took it and wrote out a death certificate there done. Sonja: In a way you are at the mercy of the hospital staff and the Dr they make these choices for you. V/O There is a way around the law for bereaved parents they can sign an affidavit saying that for cultural or religious reasons they are removing the placenta or human tissue from the hospital. Devi Can you get away with it if you sign the affidavit? Sonja: Yes Devi: So people watching this programme will say what’s the big deal? Sonja: Where’s the dignity. V/O The legal team are in the process of engaging with the Ministers involved, if necessary, Sonja is prepared to go to the constitutional court, all at her cost. Devi : Do you understand how expensive this is going to get? Sonja: I do am willing to go to highest courts to get this through this is my legacy that I will leave behind. V/O Francois and Felicia together with their sons 6 year old Francois and now 2 year old Adrian regularly visit the graves and by doing that find closure as a family Francois: I had a conversation with a lady also at 24 weeks she lost the baby she chose that she didn’t want to see the baby they must take it away that’s her way of coping with it every person has there own way of coping with it we wanted to bury our child and that should be our choice Promo 10 Is it fair to refuse parents the right to bury their baby, if born asleep under 26 weeks, this is the law in South Africa today. Promo 15 sec V/O 11 sec Babies born dead under the age of 26 weeks are treated as medical waste Meet a woman determined to give parents the right to bury their children whatever their age. Up Sound Sonja“ a miscarriage is the most unrecognized loss in our society.” Promo 3 15 sec Nicolene: How can you ever grieve knowing you baby was thrown in a bag. V/O 7 sec Bereaved parents speak out about the law that prevents them from burying their babies if born under 26 weeks.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): One woman's fight for the right of mothers to bury their chill whatever their age
metadata.Summary: “The birth of death” Sonja Smith, a Funeral Director from Centurion, is the driving force behind a forthcoming court application to challenge the law (Births and Deaths Registration Act, Act 51 of 1992) regarding miscarried babies born asleep under the age of 26 weeks of gestation who may not have a funeral and is regarded as medical waste in terms of the Waste Act. Sonja is also the founder of a non-profit company called Voice of the Unborn Baby. It has a Facebook page and has already collected 2,000 signatures in support of the proposed court case. Thursday 15 October 2015 is, internationally, Pregnancy and Infant Loss Remembrance Day, and this proposal relates to an insert that would ideally air on Sunday 11 October in order to coincide with this day.

THE LEGAL CHALLENGE Advocate Donrich Jordaan, an expert in biolaw and human rights who recently succeeded in challenging the SA Surrogacy laws and also acted for Adv. Robin Stransham-Ford in the Pretoria High Court case relating to his assisted suicide, will be representing the applicant/s in a legal challenge to the following legislation: ➢➢Births and Death Registration Act2 ➢➢Waste Act3 ➢➢Choice on Termination of Pregnancy Act4 ➢➢National Health Act5 HOW IT STARTED A hospital threw away, in the red anatomical medical waste bin, triplets born at twenty weeks of gestation in circumstances where the parents were told that the babies would have a funeral. The babies had to be retrieved from the medical waste incineration plant by the Unit Manager of the Private Hospital6. Sonja’s daughter also miscarried a baby. In France, for example, miscarried and stillborn babies are given: (i) a name, (ii) and identity number, (iii) an entry in the Population Register, and (iv) permitted to have a funeral – irrespective of the gestation period. MISCARRIAGE OR STILLBIRTH The following paragraph sets out the position in the United States: Both stillbirth and miscarriage are types of pregnancy loss, but they differ by when the loss occurs. A miscarriage (sometimes called a spontaneous abortion) is when a baby dies before the 20th week of pregnancy. Stillbirth is the death of a baby after the 20th week of pregnancy but before delivery. According to South African law it is, in both instances, the twenty-sixth week. Miscarriage has been described as “the most unrecognized loss”. Regard needs to be had to the bonding process that a mother goes through: THREE CASE STUDIES 1. Case Study #1 Felicia van Niekerk: A passionate mother who will be an excellent visual case! She lost one ‘baby’ at 25 weeks and another one at 23 weeks of gestation. Both she and her husband were fighting with everything in them to get the bodies of the ‘babies' released from the hospital for burial. She managed to obtain Death Certificates for both ‘babies'. Her Gynaecologist was Dr Ceris, near Eugene Marais Hospital in Pretoria and he was very sympathetic towards her & her circumstances. Her first baby was born in the ‘Moedersbond’ and the 2nd one at Life Eugene Marais Hospital. She now has 2 boys, aged 6 and 2 yrs old and has been wanting to do something about the current legislation for the past 5 years! Sy has a lot of ‘visuals’ at home - photo’s, sonar photo’s, memory box, etc. 2. Case Study #2 Christopher Fitchet This is the case of 2 gay men who elected to make use of the services of a surrogate mother. They were expecting twins, of which the one was born at 23 weeks and the other one at 25+ weeks. The one (Lutz) was treated as medical waste and the other one (Anja) had a dignified funeral, even though they were conceived together. They have now adopted 2 sons and were very emotional to talk about this again.. 4. Case Study #4 Nicolene Eager Nicolene resides in Pretoria East. She lost her little boy, Ryno at 22/23 weeks. Her Gynae agreed to sign the paperwork. She keeps Ryno’s ashes on her dressing table. She has a young daughter and has since given birth to another little boy
